body:
## What happens

PR #4499 (#4417) makes the Fanuc and Doosan DNM posts write the joint angles of an A-outer tilt chain (A carries B), solved from the stream pose. The machine travel check (`judge.rs::pose_problems`) judges the same joint angles.

The simulation does not follow yet. `crates/sim/src/sim.rs` (about line 636, `move_legs` rotary leg times) and the sim rotary field read the stream A/B letters, not the joint angles. So on a tilt-head machine where A carries B:
- the time estimate of a rotary move uses the wrong angle change;
- the rotary band in the simulation shows the stream letters, not the angles that the machine turns to.

The posted G-code and the travel check are correct (#4499). This issue is about the display and the time estimate only.

## Evidence

Found by the independent pre-review of PR #4499 at head `c91e47da3`.

## Done means

- The simulation uses the same joint-angle rule as the post and the check (`crates/post/src/machine/tilt_chain.rs::joint_angles`, or a shared function), so the rotary leg time and the rotary band show the joint angles.
- A test on `tilthead.mch`: a pose with A and B both turning shows the joint angles in the rotary band, and the leg time follows the joint-angle change.
- No change to posted G-code.

body:
## What happens

The generic component editor redraws a holder after a gauge-length edit in `component_edit.rs::build`. It looks up the library entry with `holder_entry` (`crates/ui/src/egui_app/state_components.rs`, about line 377). That function matches the entry by `library_ref`, id or name, not by the outline.

A user holder that carries a library name (for example a copy of "BT40 Shrink 20 mm") but has a wider body than the library entry (for example a body that the user drew or imported, hidden under the flange envelope) gets the library body at the new gauge length. The new outline can then be smaller than the real steel. Holder outlines go into the collision checks, so a check can pass when the real holder collides.

## Evidence

- Found by the independent pre-review of PR #4469 (fix for #4455) at head `1e899ad`. The route is outside the diff of #4469 and older than it.
- #4469 closes the same class of defect for the holder form and the MCP tool `edit_user_holder`: both now write through `HolderShape::component`, which refuses a shape that does not read back as itself.

## Expected

A gauge-length edit never draws a holder outline smaller than the steel that the holder had before the edit. Options:
- build the new outline from the holder's own outline (stretch or shorten the shank part) and never from a library entry found by name; or
- use the library entry only when the holder's outline equals the library entry's outline at its library gauge length, and refuse otherwise with a named reason.

## Done means

- A test: a user holder with a library name and a wider hidden body gets a gauge-length edit in the generic editor; the new outline is never smaller than the old outline at any height, or the edit is refused by name and nothing changes.
- The existing copies of library holders still edit as before when their outline equals the library outline.
- No change to toolpaths, posts or the project file format.

title: A stored Failed state for an operation: a record of the failed generation, through the history (#4245 step 2)

labels.description: Larger idea needing design or research before code

body:
## Summary

This is a step-2 item of the UI plan #4245: "A stored failed state". The maintainer accepted the step-2 items as design issues (comment of 2026-11-27 08:09 on #4245). Code starts only when the maintainer accepts the design note below. The note uses the part stamps of #4479, but it does not need them.

## What happens today

- A generation that fails returns a `CommandError`. The window shows "generate failed: …" as a refusal line, puts a marker where the generator refused (#261 part 2) and draws the moves that it made as a ghost (#261 part 3) (`land_generation`, `crates/ui/src/gen_worker.rs`).
- Nothing goes into the operation. The old cache and the old stamp stay. Thus after the refusal line goes away:
  - the Browser and the operation page show the old state: "Stale · … · 1234 moves cached", or "never generated";
  - a save and a load lose the failure;
  - MCP `generate` names the refusal one time. A later `get_job` does not show it.
- The page shows "Blocked · {why}" only for a tool problem that the tool gate finds before generation (`tool_gate::tool_problem_of`, `op_page.rs`).

The mockups E1 and E2 of #4245 show "failed" as an operation state, with its reason, in the Browser, on the operation page and in the issues pane.

## Design note (for acceptance)

### Rule 1: a failure is a record about the inputs that it saw

A failed generation writes a record on the operation:

```
GenFailure { stamp: GenStamp, message: String, at: Option<[f64; 3]> }
```

`stamp` is the stamp of the inputs that the failed run read (the same `op_stamp` that a successful run stores). The record applies only while the live stamp is equal to `stamp`. When the user changes an input, the record no longer applies, and the operation shows its normal state again (Never or Stale). A generation that succeeds removes the record.

### Rule 2: `OpStatus::Failed`

`status_of` returns a new state, `Failed`, when a record applies. The order:

1. A record applies: `Failed`.
2. No cache: `Never`.
3. The stored stamp is equal to the live stamp: `Ok`.
4. Else: `Stale`.

A new enum value makes the compiler find each `match` on `OpStatus` (about 25 places in `crates/app` and `crates/ui`). Each one gets a decision, not a default arm.

### Rule 3: the post gate refuses a failed operation

The post gate already refuses Stale and Never. It refuses `Failed` too, with the message of the record. This only adds a refusal. No program that posts today and has no failure changes. An old cache stays on screen for reference ("Failed · {why} · 1234 moves from an earlier run"), but it never posts while the record applies.

### Rule 4: the record goes through the history

AGENTS.md "Everything Is a Command": a change of the document goes through a command. A successful generation is an undo step today (`GenerateOperation`). A failure becomes the command `RecordGenerationFailure` with the same shape:

- `apply` writes the record and keeps the old cache;
- `undo` restores the old record (usually none).

One failed generation is one undo step, as one successful generation is.

The worker thread does not change. `land_generation` executes the new command in place of the plain refusal line. The refusal line, the marker and the ghost stay.

### Rule 5: the project file

`OperationDto` gets one optional field, `failure` (stamp, message, location). `PROJECT_VERSION` goes up by one. The step-up is the version alone. A save without a record writes no key, so these files keep their bytes. If #4479 lands in the same cut, the two fields can share one version step.

### Rule 6: MCP

- `generate` keeps its refusal text and stops as today.
- `get_job` and the operation list show `"status": "failed"` and the field `failure` (the message and the location). This is an addition. No tool changes its arguments.

### Rule 7: the words

The state word is "Failed" (one word, with the reason after a dot: "Failed · Pocket 1: the tool does not fit the corner R2.0"). This follows the words that #4245 accepted: "Up to date", "Needs regenerate", "fold".

### What does not change

- No toolpath and no posted G-code changes for an operation without a failure.
- `GenStamp` keeps its bytes.
- The tool gate ("Blocked · {why}") stays. It is a live check before generation.

### Options dropped

- **Keep the failure in the window state only (not saved).** This is simple. But a load loses it, and MCP cannot read it. Dropped.
- **Remove the old cache on a failure.** This makes Never and Failed the same. But the user loses the old moves for reference. Dropped: the post gate refuses the operation in all cases (rule 3).
- **Write the record without the history.** This keeps undo as it is. But it is a direct write to a document field, which AGENTS.md forbids. Dropped.

## Tests (when the note is accepted)

- A generation that the generator refuses gives `Failed` with the message. A save and a load keep it.
- An input edit after the failure gives `Stale` (an old cache) or `Never` (no cache).
- A successful generation removes the record.
- The post refuses a `Failed` operation and names the message.
- Undo after the failure restores the old state. Redo writes the record again.
- MCP `get_job` shows `"status": "failed"` and the message.
- A project without the field saves and loads the same bytes.

## Effort and safety

`effort:high`. It adds a state, a command, a project-file field and a post refusal. The post change only adds a refusal. The review must check rule 3 and that no `match` on `OpStatus` uses a default arm for `Failed`.

Done means: the maintainer accepts the design note; then one PR does rules 1 to 7 with the tests above.

Parent: #4245. Related: #4479 (part stamps), #261 (refusal location and ghost).

title: Record why a toolpath is stale: part stamps and values beside the combined stamp (#4245 step 2)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P8
labels.description: Larger idea needing design or research before code

body:
## Summary

This is a step-2 item of the UI plan #4245: "Record why a toolpath is stale". The maintainer accepted the step-2 items as design issues (comment of 2026-11-27 08:09 on #4245). Code starts only when the maintainer accepts the design note below.

## What happens today

- An operation has three states: Never, Ok and Stale (`OpStatus`, `crates/app/src/operation/types/sel.rs`).
- Generation stores one digest, `GenStamp(u64)`, in `Operation::stamp` (`crates/app/src/commands/operation/generate.rs`). The project file keeps it as `stamp: Option<u64>` (`crates/app/src/project/entity.rs`).
- `status_of` (`crates/app/src/operation/stamp.rs`) compares the stored digest with the digest of the live world. A difference gives Stale.
- The digest is one `DefaultHasher` stream. Many inputs go into it: the version salt and the law tags, the tool (`stamp_tool::write`), the parameters with the resolved heights (`OpParams::stamp_with`, `params/digest.rs`), the geometry source, the stock and the setup (WCS origin and yaw, alignment, stated rotary axes), the area controls (`op_stamp`, `boundary_ctx.rs`) and the program ahead.
- `stale_reason` cannot read which input moved. It asks the world some live questions: is the tool there, is each source there, is each picked feature there, does each height resolve, did the program ahead change. When no question fires, it says "the geometry or tool inputs changed since it was generated".

The mockup E1 of #4245 shows a reason with a value: "stock top moved Z 0.000 → Z 1.000". The fallback text does not tell the user what to check.

## Design note (for acceptance)

### Rule 1: the combined stamp stays the only judge

`GenStamp` stays the only test for Ok against Stale. The post gate and `status_of` do not change. The new records explain a Stale state. They never make one. Thus a fault in the new code can give a wrong reason, but it cannot make a stale toolpath read as current.

The combined stamp keeps its bytes. No saved project reads Stale because of this change.

### Rule 2: part stamps, taken in the same pass

A new hasher type `StampHasher` replaces `&mut DefaultHasher` in the stamp functions. It feeds each write into two hashers:

- the combined hasher, which gives the same `GenStamp` as today;
- the hasher of the current part.

The code that writes a group of inputs sets the part first. The parts:

| Part | Inputs today | Reason text (example) |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | the salt, `GENERATOR_OUTPUT_VERSION`, the law tags (#2965, #3077, #4062 and others) | "CamCraft changed how this operation is made - generate it again" |
| `tool` | `stamp_tool::write`, the wire and sinker conditions | "the tool 'EM-0600-4FL' changed" |
| `params` | the parameter values in `stamp_with` | "a parameter of this operation changed" |
| `heights` | the resolved heights (`digest::wh`, `digest::wh_opt`) | "Top moved Z 0.000 → Z 1.000" |
| `geometry` | the source placement and `geometry_signature`, the picks, the sketch digest | "the model 'Part1' moved or changed" |
| `stock` | the stock source, the stock box | "the stock top moved Z 0.000 → Z 1.000" |
| `setup` | WCS origin and yaw, the part alignment, the stated rotary axes, the machine | "the setup 'Setup 1' changed (work offset)" |
| `area` | the area controls in `op_stamp` | "the area limits changed" |
| `prior` | the program ahead (rest machining) | today's `prior_stale` text |

There is one pass and the cost is two hashers. It needs no second walk over the world.

### Rule 3: a few values, for the words "from → to"

A hash tells that a part changed, but not the old value. Generation also records some small values:

- each resolved height (the name and the Z);
- the stock box (min and max);
- the work offset origin of the setup.

The live values come from the same functions. The reason then shows the old and the new value.

### Rule 4: the order of the questions

`stale_reason` keeps today's live questions first. They are exact: a deleted tool, a deleted source, a lost pick, a height that does not resolve. Then it compares the parts in the order of the table and names the first part that moved, with values where it has them. If more than one part moved, it names the first part and adds "and N more inputs".

If every part moved, the build changed (`DefaultHasher` is stable only inside one build, as the comment on `GenStamp` says). The reason then says "CamCraft was updated since this toolpath was made - generate it again". If the operation has no part record (an older project file), the reason stays today's general text.

### Rule 5: the project file

`OperationDto` gets one optional field, `stamp_parts`, next to `stamp`. It holds the part digests and the values of rule 3. `PROJECT_VERSION` goes up by one. The step-up is the version alone: an older file has no field and reads as `None`. A save without parts writes no key, so a project without them saves the same bytes.

### Rule 6: where the reason shows

- The operation page (`op_page.rs`) shows the reason now. It gets the new text without other changes.
- The Browser row and the issues pane of #4245 (PR I) use the same function.
- MCP: the operation list says "stale". It gets an optional `stale_reason` field with the same text. This is an addition, and no tool changes its arguments.

### What does not change

- No toolpath and no posted G-code changes.
- No `GenStamp` value changes. No operation goes Stale because of this change.
- The post gate stays as it is.

### Options dropped

- **Store a copy of all the inputs, and compare it field by field.** This gives the best text. But it doubles the parameter data in the project file, and each new parameter needs compare code. Dropped.
- **Make the combined stamp the hash of the parts.** This is simpler. But each saved project reads Stale one time after the update. Dropped: rule 1 keeps the old bytes.
- **Compute the parts only when the user asks for the reason.** The old parts are not available at that time. Dropped.

## Tests (when the note is accepted)

- A height edit gives "Top moved Z a → Z b".
- A moved stock gives the stock text with the old and the new value.
- A new tool diameter gives the tool text.
- A project file without `stamp_parts` gives today's general text. It saves and loads the same bytes.
- The `GenStamp` of each recorded test project stays the same (a golden of the stamp values).
- A change of the law tag gives the `version` text.
- Each test that exists for `stale_reason` (`crates/app/tests/operations.rs`, `stamp_tests.rs`) keeps its text.

## Effort and safety

`effort:high`. The work changes the stamp code and the project file. Rule 1 keeps the Ok and Stale result exactly as it is today, so the safety floor does not apply to the judgement. The review must check that `GenStamp` keeps its bytes.

Done means: the maintainer accepts the design note; then one PR does rules 1 to 6 with the tests above, and the operation page shows the new reason.

body:
Follow-up of #2586 (the headless `camcraft-sim check`).

## Problem
`camcraft-sim check --tools` reads a T map only (`T1=6:flute=20:holder=40x50`). A `.camtools` library file is refused by name, with exit 1.

There are two causes:
- The `.camtools` reader is `parse_tool_library` in `crates/app/src/tool_library.rs`. It calls `project::tool_from_json`, which is also in `camcraft-app`. `camcraft-simview` must not depend on `camcraft-app` (#2574, answer 5).
- A `.camtools` file states no T numbers. `LibraryTool.number` is `None` for this format. The check must not guess a T number from the row order, because a wrong tool gives a wrong verdict.

## Proposal
1. Move the world-free part of the `.camtools` reader (the row reader and the tool definition reader) to `camcraft-tools`. `camcraft-app` re-exports it.
2. Give `check` a way to map each T number to a library tool by name, for example `--tools lib.camtools --tmap T1="EM-1000-4FL",T3="DR-0600"`.
3. Keep the refusal for a T number that has no tool.

## Done means
`camcraft-sim check --tools <file.camtools> --tmap ...` judges the holder and fixture laws with the library's flute, shank and holder sizes. A test in `crates/simview/tests/check/` pins it.

- Find the kernel work that is independent. Examples to examine: Z levels, separate pieces of a region, guide curve sets, entry proofs.

- The output is the same for each thread count: the moves, the notes, the fallbacks and the order of the refusals.
- The thread count has a limit. A batch of operations and one operation share one thread pool.
- A panic or an error in one part gives one clean refusal.
- The browser build works without threads.
- A cancel request stops the work.

body:
## What happens

The Fanuc post (`assets/posts/fanuc.cps`) and the Doosan DNM post (`assets/posts/doosan-dnm.cps`) write the rotary angle words under `G43.4` with the sign of the pose law.
They do not read the `signConvention` of the rotary.

A machine file can state `sign_convention: "table_rh"` on a rotary or on the machine (`crates/post/src/machine/trunnion.rs`, `RotarySignConvention`).
With `table_rh`, a positive angle turns the table right-handed about the stated axis.
That is the opposite turn of the tool relative to the work.
The two posts write the same number for `tool_rh` and `table_rh`, so on a `table_rh` rotary the machine turns the other way.

The machine check (`crates/post/src/machine/judge.rs`, `pose_problems`) also judges the letters without the sign convention.
On an asymmetric travel, the check and the machine read different angles.

No shipped machine in `assets/machines/` states `table_rh` today. A user machine file can state it.
The Mach4 post reads the convention (`assets/posts/mach4.cps`, lines 218-232).

## Found while

Found during the work on #4417 (two-rotary tilt chain). PR for #4417 refuses a rotary of an A-and-B pair that is stated along -X or -Y.
It does not change the `table_rh` behaviour. This issue holds that part.

## Done means

- Each `G43.4` dialect writes the angle with the sign of the rotary's convention, or refuses a `table_rh` rotary by name.
- The machine check judges the same signed angle that the post writes.
- A test posts a pose on a `table_rh` rotary and pins the posted sign and the check.

title: Fanuc post writes stream A/B words that a tilt-head chain (A carries B) reads as a different tool axis

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Unsafe or wrong output: gouge, collision, wrong G-code, crash, data loss; blocks a cut

labels.name: area:multiaxis

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
## What happens

The Fanuc post writes the `A` and `B` words of the stream below `G43.4` without a change.
The stream letters follow the pose law `axis = Ry(B) · Rx(A) · Z` (`crates/cl/src/cl/pose.rs`, lines 10-14).
In that law, B is the outer rotation and A is the inner rotation.

The Tilt-head machine nests the rotaries in the opposite order.
In `assets/machines/tilthead.mch` (lines 11-14), the A rotary carries the B rotary, and B carries the head.
For the joint angles A and B, that chain gives the tool axis `Rx(A) · Ry(B) · Z`.

The two products are equal only when A or B is zero.
Thus the machine reads the posted words as a different tool axis.
No check refuses the program: `cam.verify()` is clean and the post completes.

## Evidence

The review of PR #4408 measured the program `examples/catalog/multiaxis/five-axis/five-axis.nc` at head e850da857 (https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/pull/4408#issuecomment-7225976287):

- 2365 of 3357 feeds have A and B not zero.
- On 1882 feeds the two axes differ by more than 1 degree. On 1090 feeds they differ by more than 5 degrees.
- The largest difference is 27.3 degrees: `G01 X24.443 Y8.747 Z7.178 A-40.588 B68.859 F88.9`.
- With the pose law order, the deepest contact with the model is 0.054 mm. The tolerance of the operations is 0.1 mm.
- With the chain order of the machine file, the tool is up to 0.37 mm into the model, and 432 feeds are deeper than 0.15 mm.

Code on main (878f8c2f2):

- `assets/posts/fanuc.cps`, `tilt()`: writes `angleWord("A", p.A)` and `angleWord("B", p.B)` as they come. It refuses a missing letter and a reversed lone X rotary. It does not read the chain order.

The defect is not special to one case or one machine.
Each machine that states two tilting rotaries can have a chain order that differs from the pose law order.

body:
## Summary

This issue is a proposal from the two UI owners. It shows the target workspace in two mockups. It also gives the plan: the issues and pull requests that we intend to make, and the release order.

We ask the maintainer to read it and to answer the questions at the end. We do not file the sub-issues before the maintainer answers.

## Goal and limits

- CamCraft must feel like a CAM tool. A person who knows a CAM system must find the setup tree, the operation properties, Generate, Simulate and Post without a manual.
- The workspace must work on a small screen. Each side pane folds, so the viewport gets more space.
- No change in this plan changes a toolpath or posted G-code. The UI pull requests change only the look, the layout and the messages.
- Each change from the UI stays an undoable command. The MCP tools stay the same.
- Clean room: the mockups are our own drawings. We used no text, icons, layout or screenshots from another CAM product.

## Mockups

Both mockups are 1366 × 768. The source file is a FigCraft file in our design notes. They use the design language of research note 3: flat docked panes, neutral grey with a blue accent, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono (SIL OFL), and the CamCraft icons from `assets/ui/`.

### E1: all panes open

![E1: all panes open](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qsmits/Camcraft/ui-proposal-images/ui-proposal/E1-proposal.png)

- Title bar: menu bar, Save, Undo and Redo, and document tabs. The second tab shows the target. Until CamCraft can open more than one file, there is one tab. The magnifier is a placeholder for a command search.
- Ribbon: a machine-mode list ("Milling") and workflow tabs in program order: Setup, 2D, 3D, Drill, Multi-axis, Simulate, Post. The ribbon shows only the groups of the selected tab.
- Browser: the setup first (stock, machine, then the operations in program order). Each operation shows its state as a symbol and a word: current, never, calculating (elapsed time), stale, failed. "Machine: not set · Choose…" is a warning that you can click.
- Viewport: the height planes have a key with the name of the operation, and labels in the scene.
- Properties: the operation editor has six groups: Tool and cutting data, Geometry, Heights, Passes, Entry and linking, Accuracy and output. A folded group shows its values on one line. Each height shows its reference, its offset and the result: "= Z 10.000 in G54". A small text tag shows the source of each value: default, template, derived or set. A disabled button tells why it is disabled. Delete is in the ⋯ menu.
- Issues pane, below the viewport: each issue names its cause and has one button that goes to the fix. A check that did not run shows as "unavailable", never as "passed". The running job shows its elapsed time and Cancel.

### E2: all panes folded

![E2: all panes folded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qsmits/Camcraft/ui-proposal-images/ui-proposal/E2-proposal-folded.png)

- A folded side pane becomes a title chip on the viewport. The viewport then uses the full width. A click on a chip opens the pane again. The camera does not move when a pane folds or opens.
- Each chip keeps the safety state as text. The Browser chip shows the counts of failed and stale operations. The Properties chip shows the state of the operation.
- The issues pane folds to one line. The line keeps the counts and the running job with Cancel.
- The move-type key lists only the move types that the project contains. A hover tag on a move shows the operation, the move type and the feed rate.

Parts of E1 and E2 need engine work first: the source badges, the "failed" state, and a stop inside the generators. The section "Plan, step 2" names them.

## What CamCraft has today

We checked the code on `main`:

- Heights already have a reference and an offset (`HeightReference` in `crates/app/src/operation/types/height.rs`). The UI can show the result now.
- An operation has three states: Never, Ok and Stale (`OpStatus` in `crates/app/src/operation/types/sel.rs`).
- The windowed app generates toolpaths on a worker thread, with a progress overlay and Cancel (#2257). Cancel discards the result, but the worker continues to the end.
- The toolpath data has three move kinds: Rapid, Feed and Plunge (`crates/cl/src/cl/moves.rs`).
- CamCraft opens one project at a time.

## Plan, step 0: the UI kit crate

The maintainer asked on Discord to collect the UI/UX work into a crate. We propose a new crate `crates/ui-kit` (`camcraft-ui-kit`) for the design system.

- The crate depends on `egui` only. It does not depend on `camcraft-app`.
- It holds the tokens and the theme: colour roles, sizes, the theme-file reader and the contrast checks.
- It holds the components:
  - the pane frame, which folds to a title chip;
  - the title chips;
  - the ribbon cell and its groups;
  - the form row with units, the source badge and the result line;
  - the folded group with its summary line;
  - the status card for never, current, stale, calculating and failed;
  - the action band with the reasons for disabled buttons;
  - the keys for the heights and the move types;
  - the issue row.
- Each component takes plain data and returns the choice of the user. A component does not read the document. `crates/ui` keeps the panes. It changes the document into plain data, and it changes the choice into an undoable command.
- A small gallery binary shows each component in each state, in the light and the dark theme. Reviewers use it to compare the code with the mockups.

Why a crate:

1. The dependency graph makes the design rules true: a component cannot read the document, because the crate cannot see `camcraft-app`.
2. The crate compiles without flecs and the engine. Its tests (layout, contrast, AccessKit labels) run fast.
3. The look is in one place. A later palette (for example #655) maps onto one crate.

| PR | Content | Effort | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| K | Make the crate, with the decision entry for the new crate edge `ui → ui-kit` (AGENTS.md "No new dependency between our crates without a decision"). Move the theme tokens into it. Add the gallery binary. | high | R |

The later PRs build their components in the kit, and `crates/ui` keeps only the link to the app:

- B: form row, group, status card, action band.
- P: pane frame and title chips.
- D: ribbon cell.
- C1 and C2: the keys.
- I: the issue row.

We move existing code (the theme, the form seam) in the PR that touches it, never in one large move.

## Plan, step 1: UI work on what exists

These pull requests change no engine data. Each one is a `feat` PR in the enhancement lane, `P6`. Each one keeps toolpaths and posts the same, updates its `layout_page_*` and structural tests, and keeps the `crates/ui` test count (#1953).

| PR | Content | Effort | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| R | Refactor: split `panes.rs` (1665 lines) into ribbon, tabs and status bar files. No visible change. | medium | - |
| A | Theme: palette, a monospace font for numbers, the last colour literals into tokens (#1120, #4209). The tokens are in the kit. | medium | K |
| E | One command table and an in-app menu bar. The ribbon reads the same table. | high | R |
| D | Title bar with one document tab, the machine-mode list with workflow tabs, a ribbon that folds, status bar chips. All machine modes in one PR. | high | E |
| P | Side panes fold to title chips (components in the kit). The saved panel setups (#2339) keep the fold state. View ▸ Reset layout. | medium | R |

title: Heidenhain posts: write the dialect of the control and NC software stated in the machine file

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:post

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

labels.name: P6
labels.description: Accepted enhancement, not scheduled

body:
## Goal

HEIDENHAIN controls accept different program words per control and per NC software version. Today:
- the Klartext post accepts only iTNC 530 NC 340490-03;
- the DIN/ISO post writes words that are valid only on newer software (#4093, #4094).

The posts should read the control facts that the machine file already states and write the matching dialect. A control or version that a post cannot serve is refused by name.

## The machine file (no new field)

`controller.identity` already holds the facts (#3181, `assets/machines/AGENTS.md`):

```json
"controller": {
  "post": "Heidenhain Klartext",
  "identity": { "model": "iTNC 530", "nc_software": "340490-03", "installed_options": ["1", "19"] }
}
```

Proposal: keep the file to facts only. Make the values canonical:
- `model`: as HEIDENHAIN writes it (`TNC 320`, `iTNC 530`, `TNC 640`, `TNC7`, ...).
- `nc_software`: 6-digit ID, `-`, 2-digit release, optional ` SP<n>`.
- `installed_options`: HEIDENHAIN option numbers as strings.

A missing `installed_options` means "unknown": the post refuses or warns for functions that need an option.

## Capability flags (derived from model + NC software + options)

One shared resolver gives each post a flag set. The main flags, each with its HEIDENHAIN version source in the research notes:

- `language.iso`: DIN/ISO exists (none on TNC 124/128/310; TNC 320 from 340 55x-04; TNC 620 from 340 56x-02; TNC 426/430 from 280 472; TNC7 from 81762x-17).
- `blockForm`: `contour`, or `paraxial` for TNC 124/128 (one axis per block, no arcs): refuse.
- `decimals`: 3 (TNC 124/310/410) or 4.
- `toolCallByName`, `toolNameMax` (16, or 32 from TNC 640 34059x-02), `toolDefLR` (false on TNC7 from 81762x-19).
- `drill.c200` / `drill.c205`: the cycle parameter level. Q379/Q253 from iTNC 340 422. Q208/Q395 only from iTNC 60642x-04, TNC 640 34059x-04, TNC 620 81760x-01, TNC 320 77185x-05.
- `oldCycles`: cycles 1/2/17 definable, run-only (iTNC from 340 422) or absent.
- `preset.cycle247`: cycle 247 sets a datum value before iTNC 340 422, and activates a preset-table row after it.
- `dwell`: cycle 9 / `G04 F`, or `FUNCTION DWELL` (TNC 640 -07, TNC 620 -04, TNC 320 -04, TNC7; never on iTNC 530).
- `tilt` (none / cycle 19 / PLANE), `planeAxial`, `planeSym`; `tcpm.kt` / `tcpm.iso` (M128 or FUNCTION TCPM; ISO FUNCTION TCPM only from TNC 640 34059x-10 / TNC 620 81760x-07).
- `m140`, `m136m137`, `feedFzFu`, `arcs.spatial`, `arcs.helixLin`, `q.qs`, `q.qlqr`, `q.formulaPriority2020` (TNC 640 34059x-11: always write parentheses).
- Option gating: tilting needs option 8 (iTNC: 1), TCPM option 9 (iTNC: 2), and on TNC 620 cycles 201-205/208/209 need option 19.

The profile table (control and version range to flag values) is in the research notes. It covers TNC 310, 410, 426/430, iTNC 530 (four profiles), TNC 320, TNC 620, TNC 640 and TNC7.

## What the posts branch on

- **Klartext:** profile check (replaces the fixed 340490-03 check), tool call form, the `M140` retract or `L Z.. M91/M92`, cycle 247, dwell form, and later the drilling cycles and the cycle parameter level.
- **DIN/ISO:** refuse when `language.iso` is false; the G200/G205 parameter level; always `G04 F` for a dwell unless `FUNCTION DWELL` is confirmed for ISO programs; `G247` only with the preset-table meaning; the coordinate format.

## Scope and order

1. The resolver and flags in one place (post engine or a shared post helper), with a table test: control + version → flags.
2. The DIN/ISO post uses it for the fixes in #4093 and #4094 (these can land first with a narrow check, and move to the resolver here).
3. The Klartext post uses it, and serves more than 340490-03.
4. A refusal by name for an unknown model or version (no silent fallback, because cycle 247 changes meaning between versions).

## Done means

- The resolver maps each control/version in the profile table to its flags. A table test pins it.
- Both posts branch on the flags, not on fixed version strings.
- An unknown control or version is refused by name.
- The goldens of the shipped Picomax machine file do not change, except for the fixes of #4093 and #4094.

Source: HEIDENHAIN's public manuals and "Overview of New and Modified Software Functions" documents, collected and compared by the author's agent (notes, not in the repository). Related: #3095, #3181, #4085, #4086, #4087, #4088, #4093, #4094.

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
## The maintainer's words

2026-11-25: "Well we need a unifying approach to this planning and it calls for a motion planning kernel that dictates how motion can be implemented"

## Problem

Strategies have their own pass planners, link code and entry code. The same selection can give rings in one strategy and straight slots in another. A fix in one planner does not reach the others. #3743 designed a shared ring planner for 2D. This issue makes that design one kernel with a contract.

## The pipeline

1. Region: selection (edge, face, chain, points joined by lines), material side, bounds.
2. Guide curves: rings (concentric or morphed), rows, medial lines.
3. Load control: none, trochoidal, constant engagement. It changes a guide curve.
4. Order: start side (inside or outside) and direction.
5. Link: stay at depth. Lift only with a named reason.
6. Entry and exit: air entry, pre-drilled hole, cleared column, helix, ramp, arc, plunge.

A strategy is a set of choices for these stages. A strategy has no planner of its own.

## Laws

- The same region and the same guide choice give the same curves.
- The material side and the start side are separate parameters.
- The start side changes only the order and the start point.
- A fallback is visible. The status line names it.
- An entry into material needs a proof. Else the kernel refuses with a reason.
- A cut above the engagement limit is prevented or named.
- A move that migrates keeps its output. A defect fix is a separate change.

## Names

Use "path kernel" (for example `crates/motion/src/path_kernel/`). "Kernel" already means the geometry kernel and a heavy lane.

## Order of the steps

1. K0, the design record. #3750 can start at the same time, because it keeps its output.
2. K1.
3. K4 (order and link) and K5 (entry and exit).
4. K3 (load control) and K6 (move the strategies).
5. K7 grows with each step.

## Sub-issues

| Step | Content | Issues |
|---|---|---|
| K0 | Design record: stage types, laws, scope | #4024 |
| K1 | Region model: selection, material side, bounds | #4025 |
| K2 | Guide curves | #3750, #3788 |
| K3 | Load control | #4026, #3932, #3933, #3849 |
| K4 | Order and link | #3750, #3757, #3758 |
| K5 | Entry and exit | #3746, #3934, #3759, #3397 |
| K6 | Move the strategies | #3752, #3753, #3754, #3755, #3756, #3760 |
| K7 | One test suite for the laws | #4027 |

## Related issues

- Start and exit picks (#3325, #3327, #3329) stay separate. They use the start point of K4.
- #3323 is `P?`. It is only linked here.
- #3743 and #3741 are the earlier research and report.

## Scope

2D milling comes first. Then the 3D Pocket levels. 3D finishing, multi-axis, turning, sheet and EDM are not in this issue.

## Done means

Each 2D milling strategy plans through the kernel. The K7 suite is green. No strategy has its own ring, link or entry code.

body:
PathPilot Mill (`UM10587` Ch. 10) and the LinuxCNC G-code reference document extended work offsets (`G54.1 P1`..`P500`), feed per revolution (`G95`), constant surface speed (`G96 D S`), and spindle-synchronized threading (`G33 Z K`). On LinuxCNC, `G96` measures radius strictly from active WCS `X0` (never `Y`), and `G95`, `G96`, and `G33` require spindle encoder feedback (`motion.spindle-speed-in`), which servo-spindle mills such as the Tormach 770MX (`rigid_tapping: true`) provide.

Verify these behaviours on PathPilot Hub (770MX SIM) and then extend `assets/posts/tormach-mill-turn-spindle.cps` and machine capability checks:

- Record PathPilot Hub readings for `G54.1 P` index mapping (`P1`..`P6` vs `G54`..`G59`, `P7`..`P9` vs `G59.1`..`G59.3`, `P10`..`P255`), `G43 H` persistence across WCS changes, `G95`, `G96 D S`, and `G33 Z K` in Mill mode.
- Widen `workOffsetMax` and `workOffsetName(n)` in the part-in-spindle post to emit `G54.1 P<n>` up to `255` (`crates/post/src/post/work_offset.rs::MAX_BOUND`) once verified.
- Enable `G96 D<cap> S<vc>` with `G95` only on X-axis stations of machines with spindle encoder feedback and an explicit RPM clamp `D = min(machine.spindle_max, tool.max_rpm, setup.workholding_max_rpm)`. Always restore `G97` and `G94` at section end.
- Refuse `G96` on Y-axis stations and refuse `G95`, `G96`, and `G33` on machines without spindle encoder feedback.
- Enable `G33 Z K` threading when the thread hand's spindle direction matches the station's allowed direction, and refuse any mismatch by name.

Done means: PathPilot Hub readings are recorded in the PR or decision file, golden `.nc` tests pin `G54.1 P`, gated `G96`/`G95`, and `G33` output, and refusal tests pin Y-axis `G96`, non-encoder machines, unclamped CSS, and mismatched thread hand.

body:
In part-in-spindle turning, the collet nose sits at the top of the stock (`Z = -stock_stickout_mm`) and every stationary lathe tool block rides together on the mill table. A cut or rapid can drive the active tool into the collet nose, or drive the spinning stock and collet into a neighbouring tool block.

Extend turning verification (`crates/app/src/operation/turning_holder_steel.rs`, `crates/app/src/fixture_struck.rs`, `crates/tools/src/lathe_holder.rs`):

- Model the collet nose and spindle body (`Machine::spindle_d`, `Machine::spindle_len`) as revolved steel above the stock stick-out, and refuse any active tool or holder contact with `Warning::FixtureHit`.
- Support optional table positions and bounding boxes on each table tool station.
- While one station moves (rapids and feeds), check every other station's box against the swept envelope of the stock, part, collet nose, and spindle body. Emit a blocking `Warning::FixtureHit` on contact.
- Follow the unstated-limit law: when station positions or block boxes are not stated, emit a named note on the operation stating that inter-station block clearance was not judged.
- Add a non-blocking warning note when stock stick-out exceeds `3 * diameter` without tailstock support.

Done means: verifier tests prove blocking `Warning::FixtureHit` findings for collet-nose strikes and neighbouring gang-block strikes, prove clear paths pass, and confirm the not-judged note when station positions are omitted.

Add a dedicated post script (`assets/posts/tormach-mill-turn-spindle.cps`) and post routing rules (`crates/app/src/posting.rs`, `crates/app/src/posting_serves.rs`, `crates/app/src/lathe_voice.rs`):

- Emit `G53 G0 Z<safe_retract>` and a single `G43 H<stock>` once at program start. Never emit `M6` or `G49` between stations.

title: 2D Chamfer: add progressive passes across the chamfer width

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P6
labels.description: Accepted enhancement, not scheduled

body:
## Need

2D Chamfer currently cuts the full requested chamfer in one pass.

The operation calculates the final depth from the requested width and angle. It then runs the selected closed or open path at that one depth.

A single pass can apply a large cutting load to a chamfer mill. It can also reduce finish quality on a deep chamfer or on a difficult material.

Users need to distribute the chamfer over several progressive passes:

- The first pass makes a small chamfer.
- Later passes increase the chamfer width.
- The final pass reaches the authored width.
- The final part geometry remains unchanged.

This feature must not create several parallel paths at the same depth. Each pass must advance to a larger chamfer width and its matching derived depth.

## Meaning of passes

In this issue, **passes** means progressive chamfer passes across the width.

It does not mean generic Z stepdown. The Chamfer depth comes from the horizontal width and the cone angle. A separate Z stepdown could break the required cone-to-face contact.

It does not model physical tool-tip diameter, flat length, or radius. That work belongs to #895.

## Current behavior

- `ChamferParams` holds one final `width`.
- The generator derives one `break_depth` from `width * tan(angle)`.
- The generator derives one virtual-tip Z.
- The motion uses one Z level.
- 2D Chamfer has no **Passes** tab.
- The operation records one `EdgeBreak`.
- A one-pass path defines the current compatibility output.

## Proposed user interface

Show the **Passes** tab for 2D Chamfer.

Add one field:

| Field | Default | Range | Meaning |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Number of passes | 1 | 1–100 | The number of progressive chamfer passes |

Tooltip:

> The operation cuts progressive chamfer widths from the first pass to the final pass. The final pass creates the complete requested width.

A value of `1` keeps the current behavior.

Do not add a raw Z stepdown field. The user controls the final width and the pass count. The generator derives each pass depth.

## Pass-width rule

Let:

- `w` be the final authored chamfer width.
- `n` be the number of passes.
- `i` be the current pass number, starting at 1.
- `a` be the chamfer angle in degrees.
- `r` be the tip offset from #3153.

Each pass uses:

```text
pass width i = w × i / n
```

For a final width of `2 mm` and two passes:

```text
pass 1 width = 1 mm
pass 2 width = 2 mm
```

For four passes:

```text
0.5 mm
1.0 mm
1.5 mm
2.0 mm
```

The sequence always starts at the smallest width and ends at the final width.

## Depth rule

The final authored break depth remains:

```text
final depth = w × tan(a)
```

Each progressive pass uses:

```text
pass depth i = pass width i × tan(a)
```

The virtual cone-tip Z for each pass is:

```text
tip Z i = Top Z - (r + pass width i) × tan(a)
```

The tip offset stays constant through the sequence.

The operation changes the cone depth for each pass. It does not move the cutter axis farther from the selected edge on each pass.

## Pass transition

The base implementation uses a safe retract between passes.

Each pass follows this order:

1. Enter on the air side.
2. Cut the complete selected path at the pass depth.
3. Leave on the air side.
4. Retract to the retract or clearance plane.
5. Move to the next pass.
6. Enter at the next progressive depth.

The operation must not plunge directly from one chamfer depth to the next.

The lead rules from #3237 apply to each pass when that issue is available. Before #3237, the implementation must preserve the safe open-chain approach and exit from #2988.

## Closed-path rule

For a closed path:

- Passes run from the shallowest width to the final width.
- Each pass follows the selected climb direction.
- Each pass starts and ends at a valid seam.
- The operation cuts one complete loop for each pass.
- A one-pass operation keeps the exact current point order.
- Pass transitions do not create another finished edge break.

## Open-path rule

For an open chain:

- Every pass enters and exits on the physical air side.
- The final pass covers the complete selected chain.
- The cone-offset side classification remains valid at every pass depth.
- A pass that reaches model material on the air side is refused.
- A short, folded, or missing offset remains a refusal.
- The refusal names the pass and the endpoint that failed.

## Edge-break rule

Only the final pass represents the finished authored chamfer.

Record one `EdgeBreak` for each selected source path:

- The edge remains the original selected edge.
- The width remains the authored final width.
- The depth remains `w × tan(a)`.
- The slope remains `tan(a)`.
- Intermediate passes do not receive separate `EdgeBreak` records.

Stock simulation and collision checks still evaluate every generated pass motion.

This rule prevents intermediate roughing passes from receiving full finished-chamfer credit.

## Tool and safety checks

The final pass must pass the existing checks:

- The tool must be a supported chamfer mill.
- The operation angle must match the tool cone.
- The active tool radius must cover `r + w`.
- The tool flute reach must cover `(r + w) × tan(a)`.
- Every pass width must be finite, positive, and increasing.
- The cone envelope must stay safe for every pass.
- Every retract and pass transition must remain clear of the model.

The implementation may use the final pass for monotonic radius and flute-reach limits. It must still verify the actual swept motion of every pass.

The implementation must refuse:

- A pass count outside 1–100.
- More levels than the shared maximum-pass budget allows.
- Non-finite calculated widths or depths.
- A pass transition that enters model material.
- An air-side cone sweep that reaches model material.

The diagnostic must name the selected chain, pass number, conflict location, and safe correction.

## Feed behavior

Each progressive pass uses the Chamfer cutting feed.

This issue does not add:

- A roughing feed.
- A finishing feed.
- A feed reduction for the first pass.
- A separate feed for pass links.

## Proposed fix

1. Add a pass count to the 2D Chamfer operation parameters.
2. Add the pass count to the project parameter DTO.
3. Add the pass count to MCP operation create, edit, read, and job-description output.
4. Show the field on the 2D Chamfer **Passes** tab.
5. Generate cumulative widths from the first pass to the final pass.
6. Derive each pass depth from width and angle.
7. Derive each virtual-tip Z from tip offset and pass width.
8. Run the passes from the shallowest to the deepest.
9. Retract safely between passes.
10. Apply the lead rule from #3237 to each pass.
11. Keep one final `EdgeBreak` for each selected source path.
12. Reuse shared level or pass machinery only when its transition assumptions match Chamfer.
13. Update the operation guide, field help, and examples.

#1890 and PR #3220 provide prior art for progressive 3D Deburr passes. The 2D Chamfer implementation must use its own cone geometry, width law, and `EdgeBreak` law.

## Compatibility

A pass count of `1` must preserve:

- Point order.
- Z level.
- Entry and exit motion.
- Retract structure.
- Notes.
- `EdgeBreak` values.
- Existing CL and G-code goldens.

Old projects must read an absent pass count as `1`.

The default value must not add extra project JSON or digest bytes. Old readers must reject a project with more than one pass after the project-format version changes.

New readers must load old one-pass projects.

## Out of scope

This issue does not add:

- Generic Chamfer stepdown.
- Constant-depth Chamfer mode.
- Stock to leave.
- Different roughing and finishing feed rates.
- Spring passes.
- Flat-tip, ball-tip, or radiused chamfer tools.
- Per-pass tip offset.
- User-selectable level or pass links.

## Dependencies

- #2988 and PR #3059 define selected open chains.
- #3153 defines tip offset.
- #3237 defines lead-in and lead-out.
- #895 defines real physical chamfer-tip geometry.

The implementation should complete after #2988 and #3153. It should reuse #3237 for safe entry and exit when #3237 is available.

## Required tests

Add tests that prove:

- One pass is byte-equivalent to the current path.
- Two passes create increasing widths.
- A 45-degree, 2 mm final chamfer uses 1 mm and 2 mm pass widths.
- A 45-degree, four-pass chamfer uses evenly spaced progressive widths.
- Each pass depth equals `pass width × tan(angle)`.
- Each virtual-tip depth includes tip offset.
- Passes run from shallow to final depth.
- A transition retracts safely between passes.
- A closed path cuts every progressive pass once.
- An open chain enters and exits safely for every pass.
- #3237 lead settings apply to every pass.
- Only the final pass produces the finished `EdgeBreak`.
- Intermediate motion remains included in simulation and collision checks.
- Pass counts below 1 and above 100 are refused.
- The shared maximum-pass limit is enforced.
- The tool-radius refusal names the final limiting pass.
- The flute-reach refusal names the final limiting pass.
- Old projects read pass count as 1.
- A default project round-trip keeps the old bytes.
- MCP can create, edit, and read the pass count.
- The UI shows the field and tooltip.
- The guide describes the progressive-width and depth rules.

## Done means

- 2D Chamfer shows a **Passes** tab.
- The user can select 1–100 progressive passes.
- The final pass reaches the authored chamfer width.
- Each pass depth follows the chamfer angle.
- Each virtual-tip depth follows the tip offset.
- The operation runs from the shallowest to the final pass.
- Transitions retract safely between passes.
- One pass preserves the current output.
- Only the final pass records a finished edge break.
- Focused motion, app, UI, MCP, project, and simulation tests pass.
- The reached heavy lanes run on the final branch.
- The site guide documents the pass-width law.

Changelog: Add progressive passes to 2D Chamfer while preserving the final requested chamfer width.

- Default quick-op finishing contours, bosses, and frames to `Compensation::Wear` (`crates/motion/src/approach.rs`) when the active post supports cutter compensation.

  - The active post does not support `G41`/`G42`.
  - The operation cuts an open chain (`crates/app/src/operation/contour_sketch.rs`).
- Seed valid linear lead-in and lead-out lengths (at least one cutter radius, per RS-274 / ISO 6983 startup and cancel rules) so the existing lead refusal law is satisfied by default, and keep the refusal active if the user shortens the lead.
- Allow the user to switch the operation to `Computer` or `Control` in the normal parameter panel or via MCP.

Clean-room rule: based on RS-274 / ISO 6983 cutter radius compensation rules and existing `Compensation::Wear` behaviour.

**Safety floor:** changes posted `G41`/`G42` G-code and lead validation (`effort:high`).

**Done means:** a quick-op finishing contour posts `G41`/`G42` wear compensation on Fanuc, Haas, and LinuxCNC posts, falls back to `Computer` on posts without cutter compensation, refuses short leads by name, and is pinned by golden post tests.

body:
## What is needed

Users who cut simple shapes without a CAD model need a quick way to enter dimensions and make a normal operation.

## Design

- Add a `SketchRecipe` enum in `camcraft-geometry` for four shapes:
  - Rectangle with width, height, and optional corner radius.
  - Circle with diameter.
  - Obround (stadium) with length and width.
  - Regular polygon with side count and across-flats (or corner) diameter.
- Compile each recipe into exact analytic `Line`, `Arc`, and `Circle` primitives in `SketchData` (`crates/geometry/src/sketch_data.rs`).
- Refuse invalid dimensions (non-finite, zero, negative, corner radius larger than half the smaller side, side count below 3) by name. Never clamp silently.
- Store `recipe: Option<SketchRecipe>` on `Sketch` (`crates/app/src/schema.rs`) and persist it in `SketchDto` (`crates/app/src/project/sketch_dto.rs`) with a `PROJECT_VERSION` bump.
- Add `CreateSketchRecipe` and `EditSketchRecipe` undoable commands. Editing a recipe regenerates `SketchData` and marks dependent operations stale through existing stamp hashing.
- Add a composite quick-op command using `BatchCommand` (`crates/app/src/commands/batch.rs`) that creates the recipe `Sketch` and attaches a normal `2D Contour` (`crates/app/src/operation/contour_sketch.rs`, shipped in `#1864`) in one undo step.
- Ship MCP tools (`add_quick_op`, `edit_sketch_recipe`) in `crates/app/src/mcp/sketch_tools.rs` and add a compact form in the Stock/Sketch UI.

Clean-room rule: use plain machining terms only. Do not copy vendor UI labels, parameter names, or dialog flows.

**Safety floor:** generates sketch geometry that drives toolpaths and posted G-code (`effort:high`).

**Done means:** creating a rectangle, circle, obround, or polygon quick op generates, verifies, and posts G-code with no 3D model, edits in place, round-trips `.camproj`, undoes in one step, and passes MCP and UI tests.

Requested by a Discord user (PR-FPV), relayed by mkinney 2026-11-21. He runs **FluidNC** on a **PiBot** controller board on a **3040** hobby router.

## What is missing
CamCraft has Grbl, grblHAL, TinyG and Carvera posts, but no FluidNC post and no 3040-class machine file. FluidNC is grbl-derived but has its own G/M-code coverage and configuration (YAML), so the Grbl post is a guess on it.

## Clean-room sources (only these)
- FluidNC's own public documentation (wiki.fluidnc.com: supported G-codes and M-codes, tool change, spindle and coolant, probing, the YAML config).

- **Never** another CAM product's post or its output. The owner made a working post for himself with an AI from his Vectric Aspire post; that file must not be used or read for this issue.

- Program start and end, units, the safe start line.
- Tool change: `M6` support versus a stop (FluidNC can run a tool-change macro); what to write for a machine without ATC.

- Which differences from `grbl.cps` matter; reuse its structure where FluidNC behaves the same.

## Machine file
A generic 3040 router (about 300 x 400 mm work area, small spindle): `kind` mill, no ATC, travel and spindle range stated as typical and marked for the owner to confirm.

body:
## Problem

The display and graphics settings are in places that their names do not explain:

- The **Theme** door on the ribbon holds the theme, the colour-vision mode and, after #2958, the viewport line width and the anti-aliasing. Line width and anti-aliasing are not part of a theme. A user does not look for them in a menu named "Theme".
- The browser pane holds "Show origin names" (#645).
- The **Panels** (View) door holds the panel layout and the saved panel setups (#2339).
- The GPU choice is a command-line option (`--gpu`, #74).
- Other per-user choices are on the pages that use them: "Import tool holders" (#889) on the Tool library page, "Offline only" (#1945) in the AI Chat.

Each new display option must find a menu. The Theme list becomes long: after #2958 it has 18 rows.

## Proposal

Add one **Settings** window for the per-user application settings. It opens from the ribbon (a gear button at the right, near Donate), or from a menu entry. It has sections:

1. **Appearance**: theme, colour vision.
2. **Viewport / Graphics**:
   - Line width and anti-aliasing (#2958).
   - Show origin names.
   - Possible later items: the toolpath colours, the pick-highlight width, the ground grid.
3. **Graphics device** (read-only at first): the adapter and the backend that the app uses (`gpu_line`), and the sample counts that the device offers. Later, the preferred GPU (the setting behind `--gpu`).
4. **Tools and import**: "Import tool holders".
5. **AI**: "Offline only".

The Theme door can stay as a quick switch for the theme and the colour vision. Or it can open the Appearance section.

## Questions for the maintainer

1. Is the Settings window a dock panel (like Properties), or a separate window (like the tool shape window, #2397)?
2. Do the settings apply at once (as the theme picks do now), or with OK / Cancel?
3. Which settings move out of their current places, and which stay as shortcuts?
4. Does a per-user setting get an MCP tool or a CLI flag? The theme and colour vision have none today.

## Constraints

- The settings stay per-user (`prefs.json`, `view.json`). They are not in the project file and not on the undo history (#877).
- The UI rules apply: rows use the form helpers (#1122), and a page layout test is added (`layout_window_settings`).

## Done means

The maintainer answers the questions. The work is then split into sub-issues: the window, then one sub-issue for each section that moves.

## Goal

Add an opt-in compact post output mode for linear and grid pattern folders that uses local coordinate shifts (`G52`) and subprograms (`M98`/`M99` or dialect equivalent) on verified posts to reduce program size for high-count plate jobs. Depends on the pattern folder sub-issue of `#2938`.

## Scope

- **Output mode (`crates/app/src/schema.rs`, commands, MCP, project file):** Add an optional `PatternPostMode` setting on `PatternDef` with `Expanded` (default), `LocalShift` (`G52`), and `Subprogram` (`G52` + subprogram calls). Keep `Expanded` as the default so existing goldens do not change.
- **Post manifest capabilities (`assets/posts/AGENTS.md`, `crates/post/src/`):**
  - Add explicit opt-in manifest flags (`localShift = true`, `subprograms = true`) and CNC intermediate records or hooks for local shifts and subprogram calls.
  - Refuse by name any post script that does not declare the requested capability (matching `wcsRotation` and `axisInversion` refusal laws).
  - Refuse `LocalShift` or `Subprogram` for mirror folders and rotary circular patterns (a `G52` shift translates only and cannot mirror or index a rotary axis).
- **Verified dialects (`assets/posts/*.cps`):**
  - Implement and cite public control manuals (RS-274 / ISO 6983, Fanuc, Haas, LinuxCNC) for the first verified set: `fanuc.cps`, `haas.cps`, `doosan-dnm.cps`, `mazak.cps`, `mach4.cps` (`G52` + `M98`/`M99`), and `tormach.cps` (`G52` + LinuxCNC `O<sub> call`).
  - Always cancel local shift (`G52 X0. Y0. Z0.`) before every tool change, after the pattern, and at program end.

## Done means

Golden NC tests and a coordinate-interpreter verification test prove that `LocalShift` and `Subprogram` output cuts the exact same world coordinates as `Expanded` moves, cancels `G52 X0. Y0. Z0.` before tool changes and program end, and refuses undeclared posts and mirror/rotary folders by name.

title: Bore: a helical strategy (continuous helix to full depth, then a floor circle)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: claimed
labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

labels.name: area:2d

body:
### What are you trying to do

Counterbores for M6 cap screws in aluminium: Ø11 × 7 deep, cut with a Ø6 flat end mill on a small 3-axis mill (LinuxCNC, ER20 spindle). The usual way to cut these is helical interpolation: the tool spirals down on the wall radius to full depth, then runs one flat circle at the floor. It never plunges straight into solid material.

In 0.24.0 the Bore operation is a level-by-level ring ladder. At each step-down level the tool dives at the hole centre, sweeps out to the wall and runs a ring, then moves to the next level. The source describes the first engagement as the bore's centre dive, and the Lead-in tab has no entry choice for Bore. Linking → Level to level → Helix helps between levels, but that helix runs on a 1 mm radius at the centre and the first dive is still a plunge. With a 1 mm step-down that comes to 7 plunges and 7 rings per counterbore.

On a light machine, a flat end mill plunging into solid aluminium is the move most likely to chatter, pack chips or snap the tool. That's why the helical cycle is the default for counterbores and holes bored with an end mill.

### How you imagine it working

A **Helical** strategy in the Bore operation (or a separate Helical bore operation):

- The tool positions over the hole at the retract plane and descends on a **continuous helix** whose radius puts the cutter's rim on the finished wall (hole radius − tool radius − stock to leave), from Top Z to the hole floor.
- **Helix pitch** (mm per turn) is set by the user, with a sensible automatic value. Alternatively a maximum ramp angle.
- At the floor, **one full flat circle** to remove the ramp step, then a move off the wall towards the centre before retracting.
- Optional **spring pass**: a second floor circle with no extra depth.
- **Climb or conventional**, as Bore has now.
- For holes too wide for one helix to clear the core (wider than about 2 × tool diameter): helix at an inner radius first, then step out in rings at the floor, or simply refuse with a clear message.
- **Through holes:** continue the helix past the floor by the break-through allowance.

The rest of Bore can stay as it is (hole detection, per-hole floors, the reach checks).

Happy to test builds on the counterbore case above and air-cut the result on my machine.

Part of #2526 (GPU shader toolpath generation). Slice 3 of 5. Needs #2619 (CPU facet grid) and #2620 (compute seam).

Maintainer order (2026-11-18): "GPU shader issues get priority". Thus this issue is `P4`.

## What
- A compute kernel computes, for each cell of a tile, a conservative bound of the ball support height: the inverse tool offset of the facets on a grid (M. Inui, "Fast inverse offset computation using polygon rendering hardware", Computer-Aided Design 35(2), 2003; the Z-map model of B. K. Choi and R. B. Jerard, "Sculptured Surface Machining", 1998).
- f32, tile-relative coordinates. The margin is larger than the stated f32 error bound of the kernel (WGSL "Floating Point Accuracy": division 2.5 ULP, `inverseSqrt` 2 ULP). The PR states the bound and how the margin covers it.
- The CPU uses the bound only to skip facets in `support_at` (`crates/motion/src/finishing3d/support.rs` 368-388) that cannot be the highest support.
- The posted height stays the f64 `support_at` value at the true sample point. `ball_clear` (lines 132-142) stays the certifier, in f64, against every facet of the CPU grid near the ball. The GPU never removes a facet from `ball_clear`.
- The app makes the GPU result in the generate job (`crates/app/src/commands/operation/generate.rs`), once for each operation, and passes it to motion as a value. Never in a frame. The CLI and MCP use the same path.
- With no GPU, or with the GPU off, motion runs the #2619 CPU path. The result is the same bytes.

## Prime Directive
- A wrong bound can only skip the true support. Then `ball_clear` refuses the lower candidate, and the march searches higher or refuses by name. A GPU error cannot make a gouge pass. A test pins this with a deliberately wrong bound (a fault injection test).
- The tolerance is not tied to the grid resolution. The grid only filters.

## Pinning tests (CPU reference)
- GPU on and GPU off give the same `.cl` and `.cnc` bytes on the 3D finishing goldens of `crates/app/tests/golden/`. Run on the software adapter; on hardware where present.
- The fault injection test above: a bound raised by a large value gives a refusal or the same output, never a lower cutter.
- Skip and fail policy of `headless_gpu` (#615, `CAMCRAFT_REQUIRE_GPU=1`).

## Readings
Time of one large 3D finishing operation: CPU grid only (#2619) against CPU grid plus GPU filter, release build, with upload and readback times. If the GPU does not gain on the large fixtures, the PR says so and the switch stays off by default.

## Decision entry
Only if a new crate edge is added past the ones of #2620.

Effort: `effort:max` (toolpath geometry algorithm on a new compute path; safety floor).

Done means: the GPU bound filters the support scan, the goldens are byte-equal with the GPU on and off, the fault injection test passes, and the PR states the readings.

1. **Auto counts the air above the hole as depth.** The auto law reads depth as R plane - bottom. With Top Z at top_of_model (z 15) and holes starting at z 10 and 7, a 3.5 mm spot (bottom z 6.5 / 3.5) reads as 8.5 / 11.5 mm deep and resolves to a chip-break peck: `G73 X8 Y8 Z-10.5 R-2 Q18 F300` (Q = 3 x d = 18, more than the whole depth). A 3.5 mm spot should be G81 (or G82 with a dwell).
2. **No way to ask for G83.** The `cycle` choices are auto, spot, drill, peck, tap, bore, back_bore, floating_tap, ream. `peck` is always the chip-break G73; the full-retract G83 (`CycleKind::Deep`) is reachable only through auto when depth > 4 x d. A user who wants full retracts in a deep or gummy hole cannot say so.
3. **The choices are not listed.** `list_operation_types` shows `cycle` as a string with default `auto`, without the allowed words, so an agent does not find `spot` (which exists and would have served the QA run's spot drilling, see #897).

## Expected

Auto measures depth from the hole's entry (or the material top over it), not from the R plane; an explicit full-retract choice (e.g. `deep`) posts G83; `list_operation_types` lists the cycle words.

Add an external NC program simulation runner and command in `crates/app`.
It connects `camcraft-gcode` (#2217) to CamCraft's stock simulation, collision verification, and machine limit checks.

## Scope
- Depend on `camcraft-gcode` in `crates/app/Cargo.toml` and record the crate edge in `docs/decisions/` per `AGENTS.md`.
- Map each `T<n>` number from the NC file to a document tool (`tool_numbers::numbers` in `crates/app/src/tool_numbers.rs`), a `.camtools` file (`crates/app/src/tool_library.rs`), or an explicit `T -> tool` map.

- Transform NC program coordinates into world millimeters (`world = origin + sign * program_mm`), reversing `posting::wcs_context` and `post::invert` (`crates/post/src/post/invert.rs`).
- Run `camcraft_sim::stock_sim::Dexel` and `deviate` against the setup stock and optional target model, refusing setups with no stock by name (`stock_sim::stock_grid`).
- Run region-free verification laws: `verify::solid_hits` against the target model (when present), `bands_vs_fixtures_held`, and `rapids_vs_fixtures_held` (`crates/sim/src/verify/laws.rs`, `solid.rs`).
- Run `machine::judge` travel, feed, and spindle checks (`crates/app/src/machine/mod.rs`), mapping every finding to its 1-based NC line number.
- Build a `PlaySeed` (`crates/app/src/stock_play.rs`) for the parsed sections so UI playback can run it.

Depends on #2217.

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.
